claims.text: In single-crystal FeNiCrMn, yield-strength insensitivity to strain rate is driven by athermal screw-dislocation glide on {110} planes.
Local stress concentrations at pre-existing defects overcome a high Peierls barrier instead of thermal activation initiating yield.
Yield onset remains independent of strain rate until a critical stress threshold is reached.
The initial FeNiCrMn crystal may be FCC or disordered BCC, with FCC assumed for the baseline.
The initial crystal has a low density of pre-existing dislocations and no phase-transformation history.
Loading will span strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^3 s^-1 and temperatures from 77 to 600 K.
Crystal orientation should maximize resolved shear stress on {110}<111> systems if BCC or {111}<110> systems if FCC.
Use of a single crystal eliminates grain-boundary effects.
FeNiCrMn screw-dislocation segments exhibit a mild-to-wild transition governed by athermal slip.
In FeNiCrMn, screw dislocations glide athermally once local resolved shear stress exceeds the Peierls stress.
Above the Peierls stress, yielding bypasses thermally activated kink-pair nucleation.
The yield strength will remain constant within experimental error across all tested strain rates and temperatures.
Post-yield flow will contain intermittent dislocation avalanches characteristic of athermal slip.
Traditional BCC metals such as Nb exhibit thermally activated smooth flow and strong temperature or strain-rate sensitivity.
Yielding in FCC metals is typically strain-rate sensitive because of dislocation drag.
Polycrystalline FeNiCrMn may deform differently because of grain-boundary slip or phase transformation.
An FCC-to-BCC transformation under deformation has been observed in some Ti-based high-entropy alloys.
A statistically significant positive yield-strength correlation with strain rate would demonstrate that thermal activation dominates.
Detection of more than 5% BCC phase before plastic yielding would indicate that FCC-to-BCC transformation is the primary deformation mode.

contradictions.description: The baseline material is assumed to be FCC, but the central mechanism invokes BCC-like {110}<111> screw slip and a high Peierls barrier. The hypothesis does not resolve which crystal structure is present at yield or provide a corresponding structure-specific mechanism.

The conditions require an orientation that maximizes resolved shear stress on the active slip system, whereas the experiment fixes the loading direction at <111> without showing that this direction maximizes the Schmid factor for either proposed FCC or BCC slip.
